title: Saint Francis High School Receives Grant to Support First-Generation Students | Lancers in the News | Saint Francis High School
text:
Posted March 20, 2023
Saint Francis High School received a $1 million grant from The Carl Gellert and Celia Berta Foundation (Gellert Foundation) to support the school’s Holy Cross Achievers (HCA) Program, an initiative that offers students comprehensive assistance in meeting their long-term social and academic goals.
|  | HCA currently serves 60 students, all first-generation college-bound scholars from underrepresented backgrounds. Students benefit from one-on-one mentorship with an on-campus educator, student leadership formation, college readiness workshops, family connection opportunities and other forms of extensive support throughout their four years. “What we love most about the Holy Cross Achievers Program is that it provides a community for both the students and their families. We are thrilled to play a part in ensuring that this program will continue to flourish at Saint Francis High School,” said Jack Fiztpatrick, the executive director of the Gellert Foundation. |

In addition to funding capital improvements and supporting educator excellence, the Light the Way campaign continues the commitment of Saint Francis to form students in the Holy Cross tradition of educating their hearts and minds. HCA is just one of many programs established at Saint Francis that enable students to flourish in a variety of ways with academic confidence, social leadership and spiritual renewal.

About Gellert Foundation
The Carl Gellert and Celia Berta Gellert Foundation has made grants to charities all across the nine counties of the San Francisco Bay Area for nearly 65 years. The Foundation has supported numerous charitable causes over the years, from educational institutions to social services for the homeless, low-income housing, and religious, public and private school education. It has made the decision to sunset its operations in 2022. See more at www.gellertfoundation.org.

About Saint Francis High School
Founded in 1955 by the Brothers of Holy Cross, Saint Francis High School is a leading co-educational, diverse, Catholic, college preparatory school focused on educating the whole person. With a proven reputation for excellence in academics, athletics and the arts, the 118-member teaching staff prepare approximately 1,760 Saint Francis students for the rigors of college and the challenges of global citizenship in the enduring Holy Cross tradition. Saint Francis offers 162 courses in a traditional college preparatory curriculum spread across ten academic departments. Saint Francis is fully accredited by the Western Association of Schools and Colleges and is a member of the National Catholic Education Association, the College Board and the National Association of College Admissions Counselors. Located in Mountain View, California, Saint Francis High School is in the heart of Silicon Valley. For more information, visit www.sfhs.com.

title: 11 Lancers Named National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists | News | Saint Francis High School
text:
Sep 13 2024
11 Lancers named National Merit Scholarship semifinalists
|  | We are proud of these 11 seniors who were named National Merit Scholarship semifinalists: James Byrer, Simren Garg, Alexander Gklaros-Stavropoulos, Tej Nadkarni, Divya (Devyn) Ponnuvelu, Rhishi Balaa Sakthivel, Kenya Sweatt, Katie Tao, Smriti Vijay, Katherine Winton and Anvitha Yalamanchili. Congratulations! They qualified by taking the 2023 Preliminary SAT/National Merit Scholarship Qualifying Test, which served as an initial screen. The nationwide pool of semifinalists, representing less than one percent of U.S. high school seniors, includes the highest-scoring entrants in each state. The number of semifinalists in a state is proportional to the state’s percentage of the national total of graduating seniors. Go Lancers! |

title: 6-Week Progress Reports Are Available | News | Saint Francis High School
text:
Posted October 2, 2026
We've reached our first grading checkpoint of the year. Six-week Academic Progress reports were emailed to parents and students on October 1. This is a great moment to celebrate what's going well and to talk with your student about what's next.
Didn't see the email?
Progress reports come from our reporting system's email provider rather than the school's email, so they sometimes land in spam. Please check your spam or junk folder, and add brightarrow.com to your safe sender list so future reports arrive in your inbox. We're also piloting Doc Viewer in Schoology as another place to view your student's Progress Reports and Semester Report cards.
Introducing our new Grading & Progress Reports page
We know grades can feel like a big deal, so we've created a new page that brings everything together in one place. You'll find:
- How the grading year works, including our three checkpoints each semester and why only semester grades appear on the transcript
- What's in the six-week report and why some grades may still change as revisions are completed
- How progress reports connect to extracurricular eligibility

title: A School Commits to Sustainability | Lancers in the News | Saint Francis High School
text:
Posted October 27, 2025
Leaders Reflect on Saint Francis High School as a 2025 California Green Ribbon School
In 2025, Saint Francis High School (SFHS) was named a California Green Achiever, one of only five schools in the state of California to be so recognized. For school leadership, this honor signals both the culmination of a journey and the beginning of a greater one where SFHS continuously prioritizes systemic ‘green’ practices, rooted in Catholic social teaching as outlined by Pope Francis’ encyclical Laudato Si’.
Sustainable campus changes over time
Jennifer Thomas, science department chair, described how in 2019, when the school first applied for California Green Ribbon status, “We wanted to use the application, which is quite in-depth, as a benchmark and way to set goals for ourselves.” Rob Copple, a SFHS alumnus, has been involved with the facilities for over 20 years and is directly involved in the day-to-day changes that foster caring for and protecting God’s creation.

title: A School Commits to Sustainability | Lancers in the News | Saint Francis High School
text:
ourselves.” Rob Copple, a SFHS alumnus, has been involved with the facilities for over 20 years and is directly involved in the day-to-day changes that foster caring for and protecting God’s creation.
Rob shared, “I have physically changed thousands of light fixtures from compact fluorescent to LED, starting more than 15 years ago. I have also been involved with the construction and modernization of our campus to be more efficient and ‘green.’ Green Ribbon recognition is a milestone, but it is not an end.”
The Interconnectedness of Creation and the Legacy of the Holy Cross Brothers
In 2015, the Holy See published Pope Francis’ encyclical, Laudato Si’: On Care of our Common Home, which galvanized the community to commit to significant systemic changes, with the business office prioritizing expenses for environmentally friendly options such as reusable cutlery and kitchenware, which are currently utilized in the school's new dining facility. Jennifer reflected, “That document meant everything to those of us working in this space, and it gave us the wherewithal that this is our calling as Catholics.”

text:
ed in the school's new dining facility. Jennifer reflected, “That document meant everything to those of us working in this space, and it gave us the wherewithal that this is our calling as Catholics.”
Principal Katie Teekell offered, “Becoming identified as a Green Ribbon school serves as an affirmation of the work of so many: our facilities team led by Rob Copple, our Business Office— led by Sue Reyneri — and so many educators and students who have passionately worked towards living out the message of Saint Francis of Assisi inside and out of the classroom.”
For Rob, these changes align with the Holy Cross Brothers’ stewardship of the school they founded. Rob revealed that, “Through sustainability, we are carrying on the thrifty ways of the Brothers. They were the original caretakers of the school. Being in facilities, I have had the blessing of seeing how they took care of things.”

text:

Rob has also noticed a shift in the community with students utilizing dishwashing stations and consistently picking up after themselves. Rob reflected, “I think one of the greatest consequences of increasing sustainability is that it brings people together, increases overall mood, and promotes working together towards a common goal. So, being good stewards of the environment and planet, the community is also working at being good stewards towards each other.”

Faith Reignited: Caring for our Common Home on Campus
Jennifer’s commitment to observing the Green Ribbon framework on campus overlaps into both academic and personal concerns. “I want to help my students, as the youngest generation who will be most severely impacted by the rapidly changing climate, to understand scientific data and processes, as well as ways to mitigate harm and adapt to a more sustainable future.” She recently defended her dissertation at the University of San Francisco, which explored the effectiveness of the Green Ribbon School framework in K–12 schools.
Her faith has also been impacted throughout both the Saint Francis Green Ribbon journey and her own personal studies. Lately, she shared honestly, “I have experienced a reigniting of interest in Catholicity. Jesus is a role model for my approach to others. As a lifelong Catholic, I have had ebbs and flows in my relationship with the Church and faith.”

She continued, “However, with Pope Francis being the most inspirational Church leader of my lifetime and his call to Catholics in the encyclical Laudato Si', I have been inspired to listen to his call to bring the whole human family together in conversation about how we can better care for each other and the entire planetary sphere and then concrete action to achieve this.”
Regarding his faith, Rob said, “Through this Green Ribbon experience, I feel my relationship with Christ has been intensified through my own spiritual connection with the physical grounds of our campus. Today, we are all increasingly influenced by social media, technology and intangible factors. I feel that the connection and dedication to the care of our physical environment are equivalent to being connected to the flesh of Christ. This journey of the Green Ribbon has only helped to further strengthen my bond with Him.”

title: Educators | Academics | Saint Francis High School
text:
Holy Cross educators commit to students’ success in the classroom and beyond.
At Saint Francis, teachers moderate, coach or direct at least two student programs in addition to their classroom responsibilities. Many of our teachers hold advanced degrees and are experts in the fields they teach. Our faculty members believe in the Holy Cross tradition and are role models who inspire students to reach their full potential.
Whether offering guidance on a project, cheering from the sidelines at a game or creating a sense of belonging in the classroom, our educators foster a vibrant community where students feel seen and supported. Learning at Saint Francis is relational and rooted in connection—students don’t just grow academically; they thrive as part of a caring, cohesive community.

title: Schedule | Academics | Saint Francis High School
text:
At Saint Francis, our block schedule is designed to support deep, focused learning while allowing time for balance, wellness, and connection.
The rhythm of our academic year reflects our commitment to educating the whole person, with intentional breaks, spiritual life activities, and co-curricular opportunities built in. Explore how our schedule and calendar come together to create a meaningful and manageable school experience.
School Year
Our school calendar supports the mission of the school, creating intentional time and space for the spiritual, academic and social lives of students. Our calendar supports the life of the school and demonstrates the vibrancy of life at Saint Francis.
The first semester and final assessments conclude before winter break so students can truly step away from academic obligations to spend time with family. Our second semester ends before graduation on Memorial weekend.
School Day
Preparing for college starts in high school, which is why we use a uniquely designed block schedule.
Our alternating class structure mirrors a true college model, helping students transition with confidence and manage coursework effectively.

title: Accommodations Request | Details & Forms | Summer at Saint Francis | Saint Francis High School
text:
Summer at Saint Francis cares about the whole child and wants every student to succeed.
We are able to provide accommodations (such as special testing environments, preferential seating or extended time for exams etc) for any student with a documented learning disability that would require such accommodations. We do not, however, provide modifications (such as test retakes, use of notes on tests, extended deadlines for homework etc) due to the fast pace of summer coursework.
For Saint Francis students please note that equitable grading policies do not apply to our summer courses due to the pace of summer courses.
Note - Due to the fast pace of the summer term, we are able to offer a limited range of accommodations and are not able to offer modifications to curriculum, testing, homework or due dates outside of testing.
Please fill the form below to request accommodations.

title: Affording Saint Francis | Admissions | Saint Francis High School
text:
Affording a Saint Francis Education
At Saint Francis High School, we believe that a Holy Cross education should be accessible to all who seek it.
Rooted in our mission to develop students spiritually, intellectually and socially, we are committed to ensuring that financial circumstances are never a barrier to becoming part of our community.
We allocate $6.5 million in need-based grants to support our families, reinforcing our dedication to making a Saint Francis education possible for all. We understand that affordability is an important consideration, and we are here to partner with families every step of the way to make this transformative educational journey a reality.
Affordability & Financial Assistance
A Saint Francis education is an investment in your child’s future. Our tuition assistance program is designed to help bridge the gap between a family's financial resources and the cost of tuition. Tuition assistance is need-based, with the level of assistance determined through our partnership with Clarity, an independent third-party organization that evaluates each application.

How to Apply for Tuition Assistance
When considering students for admission at Saint Francis, we make no distinction between tuition assistance applicants and those who do not apply for assistance. We encourage families to apply for tuition assistance as soon as possible—do not wait for the admission decision to submit your application. Timely submission is important, as your chance of receiving assistance may be reduced if the application is submitted after the deadline, which is February 5, 2027.
There are no income restrictions for tuition assistance; all families are encouraged to apply, even if they believe they may not qualify. We understand that affordability is an important factor in your decision, and we are here to support you throughout the process. Families are required to apply for assistance each year, and as long as the student remains at Saint Francis, tuition assistance will be renewed annually based on demonstrated financial need.

text:
On behalf of all of our coaches and student-athletes here at Saint Francis, we welcome you to the class of 2030! We are excited to have you as a part of the family and hope you will consider playing a sport during your time here.
We view sports as an extension of the classroom and feel strongly about the life lessons of effort, teamwork, and sportsmanship being our definitions of success. Below is some important information about our sports programs.
Participation
Saint Francis tries to keep as many students involved in our athletic programs as possible. Last year, approximately 1200 students participated in our athletic programs.

title: Athletic Information | Class of 2030 | Saint Francis High School
text:
sports programs.
Participation
Saint Francis tries to keep as many students involved in our athletic programs as possible. Last year, approximately 1200 students participated in our athletic programs.
Some of our teams are what we call "non cut" sports. These programs (cross country, track, swimming, and wrestling) do not have a tryout period. As long as you show up every day and fulfill the team requirements, you will be part of the program. The rest of our programs have a 3 day tryout period after which the coaching staff will create the team roster. Freshman ONLY are allowed to try out for 2 "cut" sports in the same season. If you try out for one and do not make it, you will have two days to try out for another "cut" sport. A student who is not selected for a "cut" sport can always walk onto a "non cut" sport and be a part of that athletic program.
The school also greatly encourages participation in our athletic programs by being a part of a team as a manager, statistician, film crew, social media manager, or student trainer. There are many great ways to be involved!

Lancer student-athletes are more than just competitors—they are dedicated teammates, respectful opponents and faithful members of our community.
They give their all on the field, always emphasizing teamwork, effort and sportsmanship. Through their experiences, they build lifelong friendships, support one another and learn valuable life lessons that extend far beyond the game.
Off the field, our student-athletes are just as committed to their academics and personal growth. Many excel as honor students while also participating in student government, music and other extracurricular activities. At every level, they embody the values of dedication, balance, and community, striving to be well-rounded individuals who contribute to something greater than themselves.
Sport Programs Offered
Our athletic line-up comprises 31 programs with 73 teams and non-cut opportunities during every season. Many student-athletes have gone on to compete in college and professionally.

title: Band | Activities Dashboard | Student Dashboard | Students | Saint Francis High School
text:
Founded in 1955, The Lancer Band is the first and oldest organization at Saint Francis. It is the largest performing ensemble on campus and the most easily recognizable!
The Lancer Band and Color Guard has received countless accolades and awards throughout its storied history. It is the heart of all campus events, including rallies, sporting events, liturgies, and celebrations. Become a part of the tradition and cement your place in history!
Our Ensembles
Concert and Symphonic Bands
The Concert Band welcomes all wind, brass, and percussion students who are joining band for the first time at Saint Francis. Concert Band participates in the Winter and Spring Concerts, one CMEA festival, and Lancer Marching Band. This ensemble is the prerequisite course for entry into Symphonic Band.

title: Band | Activities Dashboard | Student Dashboard | Students | Saint Francis High School
text:
time at Saint Francis. Concert Band participates in the Winter and Spring Concerts, one CMEA festival, and Lancer Marching Band. This ensemble is the prerequisite course for entry into Symphonic Band.
The Symphonic Band  premiere wind ensemble at Saint Francis High School. One year experience in Concert Band is required for entry into this ensemble. In Symphonic Band, music theory, history, aural skills, and performance are explored at greater depth through performance. This ensemble hosts four concerts annually, performs locally at colleges and community events, participates in CMEA festivals, and are members of the Lancer Marching Band.
Concert Band and Symphonic Band are classes and meet during the school day. Both ensemble classes fulfill UC-F Fine Art graduation requirements.
Lancer Band and Color Guard
The Lancer Marching Band is the oldest campus organization, dating back to the founding of the school. It is the largest performing ensemble on campus and the most easily recognizable! Saint Francis High School is the only WCAL school with a competitive field show band and has received many accolades in its long and proud history.

ensemble on campus and the most easily recognizable! Saint Francis High School is the only WCAL school with a competitive field show band and has received many accolades in its long and proud history.
All members of Concert Band and Symphonic Band are required to participate in the Lancer Band as part of their study of music. The Lancer Band performs at football games, school rallies, community parades, and campus events. As a competitive marching band, this ensemble attends competitions and showcases each year.
The Lancer Band is a co-curricular ensemble and meets weekly on Wednesday evenings and Saturdays through mid-November. Band camp is hosted annually at the beginning of August for all students.
Color Guard and Winter Guard
The award-winning Saint Francis Lancer Color Guard is the primary visual element of the Lancer Band and Color Guard, using dance choreography, flags, prop rifles, and prop sabers. This dynamic group combines the grace and athleticism of dance and rhythmic gymnastics into one unstoppable performance! Color Guard meets weekly with Marching Band Wednesday evenings and Saturdays during the fall.

Choir uplifts student voices in both an ensemble and solo setting. Let your voice be heard and join choir today! Our choir program uses music to learn about the larger world – we regularly sing in other languages, including Spanish, Hebrew, Middle English, Latin, Croatian, and Hawaiian.
Our Ensembles
There are two ensembles within the Choir program. Treble Choir offers first-time choral singers the opportunity to learn about music with their peers in a welcoming environment and gives them several chances to perform throughout the year. Chamber Choir welcomes returning students and gives them opportunities to perform additional songs at concerts and events.
Choir performs at a minimum of six times per year, including Open House, the Fall Concert, the Winter Concert, St. Patrick’s Seminary Alumni Concert, the March Concert, and the May Concert.
Choir regularly receives Gold ratings at festivals.

Come Travel With Us!
Many students love participating in our music program because of our fantastic travel opportunities every year. All enrolled members of Treble Choir or Chamber Choir are eligible to travel annually! Our ensembles travel on a rotating basis to Los Angeles, domestic destinations, and international tours, performing at renowned venues and receiving masterclasses from decorated artists. Clubs & Activities

| 3-D Printing Club Moderator: Ms. Mei Yang Ever wanted to take an idea from your head and turn it into something real you can actually hold? Welcome to the 3D Printing Club — the place to get hands-on time with design software and 3D printers. We’ll teach you everything step-by-step so you can start bringing your own 3D models to life. Join us and see what you can create! No experience necessary. All are welcome! AI/ML Moderator: Mr. Mike Chechelnitsky Learn the workings of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, and help members participate in competitions. ASL Club Moderator: Ms. Sarah McBride  \|Mr. Patrick Kelly ASL Club is a club wants students to learn about ASL, deaf culture, and being an advocate for people who are deaf. Students don't have to know any ASL to be in the club and attend club meetings. The point is to learn about the Deaf community and learn signs. It's to highlight deaf experiences, events, and even modern day activities that are happening constantly in the deaf community. Audio/Visual Club Moderator: Mr. Dale Thompson A/V Club’s responsibilities are to set up and run the liturgies, rallies, and other activities such as the night of acoustics, or dance showcase. We run the sound systems, the light systems, and the presentations or projections. Aviation & Transportation Club Moderator: Mr. Brian Wahl Learn about the physics, history, and technology behind flight. Starting this year, we're also covering rail and ships. For each mode of transportation, we'll cover their past, present, and future. In addition to meetings on campus, we'll also be taking field trips to museums, airports, and rail depots. Baking Club Moderator: Mrs. Joy Anderson Baking Club members engage in baking themed activities through watch parties, decorating events, baking contests, and monthly at-home theme baking challenges. Book Club Moderator: Ms. Ella Hadrovic Come join Book Club for a fun, inviting space to discuss what we're reading and connect with people who share our love of books. We don't have required reading, but we recommend books across genres and create literary crafts together. Bring Change To Mind Moderator: Mrs. MaryLynne Rodriguez Bring Change to Mind is a National Organization, created to bring awareness and conversation to mental health and reduce stigma in high school communities. Build and Design Club Moderator:Mr. Chihiro Ikezi Learning build and design through lego building, gingerbread house contests, and point-perspective workshops. Calligraphy Club Moderator: Ms. Karla Andrade Galvan The Calligraphy Club is a creative space for students to explore the art of beautiful writing and lettering. Chess Club Moderator: Mr. Terry O'Donnell We provide the opportunity to play and learn more about chess. Cooking Club Moderator: Mr. Michael Pilawski \|Mr. Winston Wint \|Mr. Tim Yang Cooking Club is a group of students who get together 8 times a year after school, learn a recipe from our amazing hospitality staff, cook the recipe and then eat it. Come join the fun! Crochet Club Moderator: Dr. Sean Gross The Crochet Club meets after school and gives students and educators a space to share our passion for crocheting a variety of items from plush toys to blankets. Everyone is welcome regardless of experience level. If you are brand new to crocheting, we will help you get started and encourage you along the way! Economics Club Moderator: Mr. Cade Nethercott For students who want to learn about Economics while playing a variety of games. Environmental Club Moderator: Dr. Kim Taylor Our club is committed to expanding our understanding of environmental issues. We work to educate our St Francis community and raise our school's standard of sustainability through hands-on activities. Our biggest event is Earth Week. Fellowship Of Holy Cross Athletes Moderator: Mr. Michael Pilawski Come share your faith journey with other Saint Francis athletes in a collaboration setting. The group meets once a month for donuts, juice and fellowship. Film Club Moderator: Mr. Don Carroll Film Club is a casual group of students who are interested in the art of filmmaking. We meet to watch a film as a group, and then have a discussion afterwards. FMSA (Future Medical Students Association) Moderator: Mr. Philip Pompei Future Medical Students Association (FMSA) is a club committed to helping students explore the various medical fields in anticipation of medical school. We bring in local health care professionals to educate our club members and host at least one on-campus blood drive per year in partnership with Red Cross. Girls Who Code Moderator: Ms. Joanna Vollucci Girls Who Code strives to increase the representation of women, transgender, and non-binary individuals in technology and to break down the gender barriers that exist in society and the industry. Our goal is to create safe, inclusive spaces and provide opportunities for people of all genders to explore and engage with various Computer Science topics! Guitar Club Moderator: Mr. Chihiro Ikezi Social club that invites all musicians of any level to jam on Fridays after school. Ignite (Youth Group) Moderator: Mr. Chris Mardesich \|  Sr. Jodi Min IGNITE is our school's faith-based youth group, run by a core team of students and our Co-Moderators. Founded as a Catholic/Christian space to openly share faith, this group is open to all students of any background to find a space to find community and fellowship. A typical night has free dinner, games, music, a personal sharing, and small groups. We also host on-site Day Retreats such as ENCOUNTER and PATHWAYS. IGNITE is a space where you can be real and belong. Injury Prevention Club Moderator: Ms. Isabelle Alduino The Injury Prevention Club promotes safety and helps people learn how to prevent common injuries. IPC members learn about proper exercise techniques, stretching, nutrition, and the importance of specific daily habits. The club also focuses on the mental challenges of being injured, and provides a support space throughout the recovery process. Intramurals Moderator: Mr. Ralph Fullerton Intramurals give students the opportunity to enjoy sports, build friendships, and stay active in a fun and welcoming environment. Designed for all skill levels, intramural activities focus on participation, teamwork, and school spirit rather than competition. Students can participate with friends, meet new people, and enjoy a variety of sports throughout the school year. It’s a great way to get involved and be part of the Saint Francis community! Lancer Analytics Moderator: Mr. Mike Chechelnitsky Partnering with our athletics teams to use data science principles to assist tactical and performance analysis. Lancer Gaming Club Moderator: Mr. Ralph Fullerton Lancerhacks Moderator: Mr. Neil Swank Plan the annual 12 hour Hack-a-Thon in March. This year will be the 10th anniversary of this event. We release a monthly newsletter that publicizes internal and external tech events. We also run mini-hacks throughout the year. Lancers LEAP Innovation Program Moderator: Mr. Bill Beasley We empower our community to build a future that reflects both courage and compassion. Through hands-on experiences, we guide students, educators and partners to approach challenges with resilience, purpose and an unwavering commitment to meaningful impact. Lancer Radio & Podcasts Moderator: Mr. Dale Thompson   \|Mr. Bill Beasley A school podcast for any and all topics, fully run by student volunteers! Supports our LEAP program and our library Oral History program as well. Lancer Studios (Live/Production) Moderator: Mr. Matt Ross Home of all Student Broadcast and Video Media Math Club Moderator: Coach Vanessa Staton We prepare for and participate in competitions including AMC, BMT, and SMT. We talk about interesting topics that are in these competitions and work through example problems together. Mind-Body-Spirit Moderator: Ms. Rachel Safier At Mind, Body, Spirit, we practice self-care as well as deepen our knowledge of mindfulness through different relaxation techniques. Our mission is to connect people through activities such as tai chi, art, and meditation. Mind, Body, Spirit is a safe space for people to step away from the everyday stress of school and foster new relationships while learning to express themselves and their identities. Mindframes / Creative Writing / Café Mots Moderator: Ms. Nancy Yang We are a student-run literary magazine that publishes student art, poems, and stories. We gather to create and share our work, and to make decisions about our magazine for publication in the spring. Model United Nations Moderator: Mr. Zachary Herhold \|Ms. Ning Yang Saint Francis's Model UN is a club where students will gather to simulate the work of the real United Nations. When students participate, they will often be asked to assume the role of a country and then represent that country and its needs in each simulation. These conferences are a fun and lively way for students to learn the basics of research, grow more comfortable with public speaking, practice creativity, collaborate with their peers, and help solve many of the world's most pressing issues. Students learn the basics of the activity here on campus and then travel 3-4 times a year to conferences around the Bay Area. Multicultural Showcase Club Moderator: Mrs. Theresa Orozco  \|Ms. Yajaira Morales The Multicultural Showcase Club is dedicated to highlighting and celebrating the rich cultural tapestry of our school community. Each year, our members collaborate to host an annual showcase that brings students together through the universal language of performance and storytelling. Newspaper Moderator:  Mr. Don Carroll  \|Ms. Amy Sherrard The Lancer, the student newspaper, is an online publication that allows students to express their journalistic interest in current events, art and culture, sports, and school events through writing, art and photography. It's an excellent opportunity not only to produce a quality student publication but also to develop leadership skills, as students can occupy many different organizational roles requiring responsibility. OC3AN (Ocean Activity/Appreciation/Activism Club) Moderator: Mr. Michael Rubin The Ocean is calling and I must go! Paint Box (Art Club) Moderator: Mr. Ben McEvoy Paintbox, the Saint Francis Art Club. Come create with your fellow Paintbox members! Photography Club Moderator: Ms. Amy Sherrard Quantum Computing Club Moderator: Mrs. Kerry Lewis Quantum Computing Club is a space for curious students to discover the future of computing. Through projects, discussions, and teamwork, members build a strong foundation in quantum concepts while having fun learning together. Quiz Bowl Moderator: Mrs. Elise Bibriescas Quizbowl is a fast paced, buzzer-based game in which players answer questions across various categories. For example, the questions could be from literature, history, science, pop culture, music, and many others. Teams of up to four students compete against other regional teams to qualify for the national tournament that occurs in May in Atlanta. Over the past two years, Saint Francis has achieved deep playoff runs, securing a highest of 21st place nationally at the tournament in 2025. Overall, quizbowl is a great opportunity to have a lot of fun, explore new areas, and build an amazing community together! Robotics Moderator: Mr. Addison Raak Lancer Robotics is the FIRST Robotics Competition team at Saint Francis High School in Mountain View, CA. We pride ourselves in cultivating an engaging environment where students of all classes are provided the opportunity to collaborate with each other alongside experienced mentors with careers in STEM. When we're not engineering our competition robot, Lancer Robotics runs off-season workshops, provides community support through local outreach with our neighboring St. Simon schools, and fosters a strong team dynamic by hosting inter-team events like our annual Minibots competition! Science Bowl Moderator: Mr. Chidozie Onuegbe Club geared towards spreading healthy competitive appreciation towards STEM Science Olympiad Moderator: Contact Mr. Lucas Science Olympiad is a national STEM competition to challenge students across a wide variety of subjects. Members choose which events they want to compete in, and collaborate in groups to either study for their subject, or build their submission. Competitions go throughout the year and do require competing members to travel around the Bay Area, possibly farther. Service Club Moderator: Mr. Sean O'Niell Our mission is to unite the school community through meaningful service, fostering compassion, collaboration, and a commitment to making lasting impact in our community and beyond. By hosting monthly service events, we aim to inspire every student to take action and develop leadership skills by serving others. Social Business Club Moderator: Mr. Chidozie Onuegbe A club geared towards expanding knowledge of the financial sector and working in business Speech & Debate Moderator: Mr. Thomas Woodhead. \| Mr. John Foy \| Dr. Sean Gross SFHS Speech & Debate gives students the opportunity to develop confidence, communication skills, and critical thinking through public speaking and competitive debate. Students explore current issues, research a variety of topics, and learn to effectively present and defend their ideas. Whether you are an experienced speaker or new to debate, the team welcomes students of all experience levels who are ready to learn, grow, and find their voice. Students also have opportunities to compete in tournaments throughout the year. Sports Medicine Club Moderator: Ms. Isabelle Alduino The sports medicine club provides students with opportunities to learn about different professions, skills, equipment, and more that exist in the sports medicine world. Meetings will be directed by the students and led by the moderator, so bring all of your medical interests and we can explore them. Artists and performers can take the stage at the International Showcase or our Night of Acoustics, while aspiring poets are invited to share their work at Café Mots. Code of Conduct: AB 500
Assembly Bill 500 (AB500), effective January 1, 2018, adds section 44050 of the California Education Code, which requires schools to provide the section on employee interactions with students in its code of conduct, to parents and guardians of enrolled students on the School’s website.
As a school that has consistently followed strict protocols on hiring educators as well as adhering to clear expectations for their interaction with students, we welcome the opportunity to share with you our school policies. Below is a consolidation of policies from our educator handbook that deal with hiring, training, code of conduct, mandatory reporting and specific guidelines on situations of potential impropriety. These policies are also accessible on the parent and student portals.
Please know that our students’ safety is our top priority. We are committed to placing caring and respectful staff in our classrooms, offices, fields and courts. We understand the great gift of your children, and they are always at the forefront of everything we do.
In gratitude,
Katie Teekell ‘00
Principal

Guidelines for Safeguarding
Furthermore, educators are not only trained on but required by law to act in the best interest of the student in suspicious situations.
All school employees are mandated reporters who are required, by law, to report all known or suspected cases of child abuse or neglect. Mandated reporters must not attempt to investigate whether the allegations are valid. If child abuse or neglect is reasonably suspected or if a student shares information with a mandated reporter leading him/her to believe abuse or neglect has taken place, the report must be made. No supervisor or administrator can impede or inhibit a report or subject the reporting person to any sanction.

title: Code of Conduct | Saint Francis High School
text:
ter leading him/her to believe abuse or neglect has taken place, the report must be made. No supervisor or administrator can impede or inhibit a report or subject the reporting person to any sanction.
To make a report, an employee must contact an appropriate local law enforcement or county child welfare agency. This legal obligation is not satisfied by making a report of the incident to a supervisor or to the school. An appropriate law enforcement agency may be a Police or Sheriff’s Department or County Child Protective Services.
The report should be made immediately over the telephone and should be followed up in writing. The law enforcement agency has special forms for this purpose that they will ask you to complete. If a report cannot be made immediately over the telephone, then an initial report may be made via email or fax.
Finally, SFHS employees are provided with specific situations to avoid in order to avoid the incidence of impropriety.
The following are expectations to establish boundaries and avoid the appearance of impropriety:
- Do not stay alone in a room with a student unless there is a window permitting others to view the room or the door is open.

title: Code of Conduct | Saint Francis High School
text:
ectations to establish boundaries and avoid the appearance of impropriety:
- Do not stay alone in a room with a student unless there is a window permitting others to view the room or the door is open.
- Do not allow students to become overly friendly or familiar with you. Students should never call teachers by their first names or nicknames.
- Do not engage in private correspondence with students. Always use your school email account when corresponding with students. If you receive personal communication from a student and the communication is not appropriate, keep a copy of the communication and inform your supervisor.
- Do not visit students in their homes unless their parents are present; do not invite students to your home.
- Do not transport students in your own vehicle.
- Do not take the role of a surrogate parent with a student; do not criticize a student’s parents to the student.
- Do not give students your home or cell phone number without the knowledge and permission of your supervisor.
- Do not hire students to work in your home without the knowledge and consent of your supervisor.
- Do not discuss your personal issues or problems with your students.

Helping to Support & Empower Students
At Saint Francis, we believe the journey beyond high school is a deeply personal one, shaped by each student’s values, passions, and aspirations.
Rooted in the Holy Cross tradition, we guide students to reflect on who they are, what they care about, and how they hope to serve the world. From that foundation, they explore colleges, universities, and other meaningful opportunities that align with their goals.
We welcome students and families into this process, encouraging open conversations and exploration. Sophomores connect with their college counselor to build a relationship of trust and guidance that will continue through their senior year. Rather than focusing immediately on applications and test scores, we take the time to understand each student as a whole person—empowering them to move forward with confidence, purpose, and a sense of possibility.

| Welcome to the Parent Highlights & Insight Corner! In continuation with our focus on social emotional learning, we want to recognize the importance of your student’s character traits and how it relates to college admissions. In recent years, college admissions offices have relayed the importance of character assessment within college admissions. (More information about the Making Caring Common Project from Harvard University can be found here.) With this in mind, on three occasions during your student’s high school career, the Counseling Department will reach out to parents/guardians to gather information that will help your student’s counselor learn what drives your student. These short surveys will occur at the end of sophomore year, the end of junior year, and the beginning of senior year. Each survey will ask a few questions that will allow you to share anecdotes that will help your student’s counselor to better understand your student and their individual strengths and motivations. Examples of character traits include: Compassion Curiosity Gratitude Grit Growth Mindset Initiative Integrity Optimism in the face of adversity or challenge Perspective-Taking Purpose Resilience Respect Self Awareness Selflessness Self Management Thoughtful Decision Making During the senior year, counselors use the information provided from these parent responses, anecdotes from teachers/coaches, and individual meetings with students to compose a counselor recommendation letter that demonstrates your student’s unique motivations and strengths. Posted December 9, 2025
Dear Saint Francis Families,
As we near the end of the semester and move through the season of Advent, we’re reminded of the many ways this time invites us to slow down, reflect and prepare for moments of togetherness as a family. Our Christmas with Saint Francis celebration grounded us in hope, peace, joy and love of the season.
As we look ahead to the upcoming break, we know our students are also working hard and turning their attention to final assessments. While the holidays bring excitement and joy, they can also make for busy schedules. We are especially grateful for your partnership in helping students remain present at school during these important days. Being on campus for finals in December not only supports their success but allows students the gift of truly resting and stepping away from schoolwork during our vacation days in January.
End of Semester Schedules
We believe that students can demonstrate knowledge and skills in many ways. As such, for final assessments, students will have a combination of projects, performances, essays and exams.
- This week we work to conclude most of the final projects.

2026-27 Book Purchases
Saint Francis continues to partner with BNC (formerly MBS Direct), one of the largest distributors of new and used books in the nation. BNC provides a service that makes the process of ordering textbooks easy, efficient and cost-effective. BNC will maintain a list of the course offerings and the books and materials for each course. BNC will also reference the ISBN number for each book.
Please note: If a course does not require any books or the course is using an Apple iBook purchased through iTunes, a corresponding message will display that materials will be provided at a later date or purchased at a later date. Some courses will provide additional book lists on the first day of class. These will not go through BNC.
With the exception of the Apple iBook textbooks, students are welcome to purchase books from any vendor. Should you desire to use another vendor, please be careful to record the necessary textbook information, including ISBN number, prior to contacting any other textbook vendor.

Attendance
Because of the short time span of 2.5 weeks into which an entire semester of content is compressed, attendance is critical. Therefore, in order to receive credit for a semester course, a student may be absent (not present in class or missing more than 30 minutes of class) no more than 1 day of the semester.
Furthermore, a student may be tardy (late by 30 minutes or less) no more than 3 times, as 3 tardies constitutes an absence. Thus, if a student is late on 4 or more days, or absent for 1 day then absent or late on an additional day, the student cannot receive credit for the course.

Policy for Scheduling an early Final Exam
An individual student’s final exam may not be rescheduled, unless it is for an extreme situation. In order to maintain the integrity of final exams, all students must take them at the same time. Final exams occur the last day of any term.

Our Recitals
Winter Dance Showcase
Every first semester, the Winter Dance Showcase gives students in dance classes and clubs the opportunity to produce a dance performance. Now in its fourth year at our school, the showcase has already become a cherished tradition. Open to students of all levels and backgrounds, the event features a variety of styles—including jazz, tap, hip hop, ballet, Folklorico, Bollywood, K-pop, and Tinikling.
UDC Recital
Unity Dance Crew’s Recital is the spring semester dance show featuring dance classes and clubs. As a completely student-run production, it allows students to create their own choreography, select their outfits, music, and lighting, and curate the program. The show honors senior dance students by giving them the opportunity to showcase their talents in a final solo performance. As an annual production, it represents the culmination of a tremendous amount of work from dance students on campus.

Biennial Band/Dance Concert
The first-ever band and dance concert took place in March 2024, uniting students from both band and dance classes. Participants performed in small ensembles and created original choreography set to the music played by their classmates. They also coordinated outfits, stage space, and tempo. It was a fun experience for everyone. Be on the lookout for next year's concert in 2026.
International Showcase
The International Showcase is a variety show hosted by the International Club. As the culminating event of Multicultural Week, students and clubs are invited to showcase their talents and ethnic backgrounds in any form they choose, such as singing, playing an instrument, reciting a poem, or dancing. Many dance clubs on campus participate and demonstrate dance styles from their cultures.

We are incredibly intentional in our scholastic programming and experiences. Our various courses and departments allow the freedom of learning and exploration for each student.
“Even though we base our philosophy course on the data of faith, no one need fear that we shall confine our teaching within narrow and unscientific boundaries. No, we wish to accept science without prejudice and in a manner adapted to the needs of our times. We do not want our students to be ignorant of anything they should know. To this end, we shall shrink from no sacrifice.”
Blessed Basil Moreau
Circular Letter 36; 1849

Lancers build strong foundations through diverse pathways that foster confidence, mathematical reasoning and creative problem solving.

During spring trips, Lancers can put their passports—and their learning—to work in France and Taiwan. Our Saint Francis Hospitality Team is dedicated to providing fresh, healthy and delicious meals for our community. We prioritize seasonal, local and organic ingredients, preparing everything from scratch—from stocks and soups to dressings and sauces.
Sustainability Commitment
We strive to eliminate waste and reduce our environmental footprint by:
- No Single-Use Items – We serve meals with reusable trays, utensils and cups, minimizing plastic waste.
- Sorting Waste Properly – Every dining area includes recycling, compost and landfill bins to ensure waste is disposed of responsibly.

text:
Dramatic Arts at Saint Francis is one of the best in the area. Our outstanding theatre program offers a unique opportunity for students with varying interests in theatre by providing countless opportunities for on and off-stage participation.
Students interested in drama have the opportunity to partake as actors (leading, supporting, featured, and ensemble roles), designers (lighting, sound, and costumes), and creative team members (student directors, choreographers, vocal directors, and stage managers).
Sarah Vorrath ‘22, Yasmine Bari ‘21, Graciella Butler ‘21, and Gabriella Federighi ‘22 invite the audience in to “be their guests” in Beauty and the Beast Jr. Actors and Crew worked tirelessly to help create 2021’s semi-virtual Spring Musical.
Saint Francis Dramatic Arts takes pride not only in building a strong theatre program but also in building a strong community within. If you want to be a part of quality productions, prepare for college auditions, or even pursue a career in theater or television, then Saint Francis drama is the place to be!

Our Productions
Fall Musical
New for the 2025-2026 school year, the Fall musical will occur at the very beginning of the semester with auditions and callbacks the first week of school. The production will be based in the utilization of acting techniques and exploration of ensemble work. This small cast show will perform in the Innovation BlackBox Theatre and allow students to deep dive into the roots of the story, examining how to tell a story when the theatrical elements are stripped to their “bare bones”.
The cast strikes their ending pose post a “Dancing Queen” encore in 2022’s Mamma Mia! This exciting show was sure to get audiences dancing to ABBA’s hit tunes!

Fall Play
The Fall Play occurs each year in the first semester. The production allows students to experience putting on a non-musical production, and for the actors, focuses on learning and implementing acting objectives and tactics that will help with their overall character development and drama education. Past fall productions include, “Rumors” (2024), “A Gift To Remember” (2023), “The Sparrow” (2022), “A Little Princess” (2021), and "Blithe Spirit" (2019).
Student-Directed Musical
The Student-Directed Musical occurs every year in between the Fall Play and Spring Musical. The “Student-Run” (as it is commonly referred to) is a production put on entirely by students, with little to no faculty help. Students are encouraged to apply to direct and pitch a musical during the spring semester. Past Student-Run productions include, “The Lightning Thief” (2025), “Freaky Friday” (2024), “Little Shop Of Horrors” (2023), “9 to 5: The Musical” (2022), and “Bright Star” (2021).

Spring Musical
The Spring Musical is performed in the latter half of the spring semester, with auditions following the close of the Student-Directed Musical. Nearly 75 students participate in this production which includes large casts, a complete stage crew, student choreographers, costume designers, a technical crew, an orchestra, and many more. Past shows include “High School Musical" (2025), “Footloose” (2024), “Legally Blonde: The Musical" (2023), "Mamma Mia!” (2022), and “Beauty and the Beast Jr.” (2021).

title: Emergency Info | Saint Francis High School
text:
Emergency Procedures for Parents and Guardians
The safety and well-being of our students is our top priority. In the event of a disaster during school hours, our administration will determine the best course of action to manage the health and safety of everyone on campus.
Communication & Updates
- Updates will be sent via our Emergency Notification System (voice mail, text and email). Additional messaging will be posted to our website and social media channels.
Student Supervision & Release
- Educators will remain with students until they are picked up by a parent or an authorized adult listed on the School Closure/Emergency Release Form. Please ensure that your carpool driver is included in your pre-authorized list if you want your child to be released to them in an emergency.
- Saint Francis has emergency food and water supplies for students who may need to stay on campus.
- Educators are trained in first aid, security, rescue and emergency communication.

title: Emergency Info | Saint Francis High School
text:
in an emergency.
- Saint Francis has emergency food and water supplies for students who may need to stay on campus.
- Educators are trained in first aid, security, rescue and emergency communication.
Emergency professionals have reviewed our emergency plans and trained our staff. We will continue to receive training in conjunction with the Mountain View Police Department, as part of a program called “The Silicon Valley Safe Schools Consortium.”
Important Reminders
- Do not call the school—phone lines must remain open for emergency communication. Information will be shared with parents when available and safe to do so.
- Check for updates before coming to campus: Parents will receive instructions from our Emergency Notification System (voice mail, text and email). Additional messaging will be posted to our website and social media channels.
- Avoid calling your child’s cell phone, as networks may be down, or overwhelmed and additional noise may put them at risk in a lockdown situation.
By following these guidelines, you help ensure a safe and organized response in an emergency.

Advance Planning for Emergencies
- Keep Emergency Forms Updated: Submit a new school Emergency Form whenever you change your phone number or address.
- Review the School Closure Emergency Release Form: Ensure authorized pickup contacts (including carpool drivers) are current.
- Verify Contact Information: Keep phone numbers and email addresses up to date to receive emergency notifications.
- Create a Family Plan: Discuss and prepare how your family and friends will support each other in a crisis.
Understanding Safety Procedure Terms
Safety procedures are defined based on the type of emergency. It’s important for our families to know the definitions, understand what happens on campus during these situations and follow the outlined instructions.
Shelter in Place
A shelter in place is used when there is no immediate danger to our school but conditions off campus may pose a risk. This means it’s safer for students and staff to stay indoors.
Examples include:
- A police situation in the neighborhood

title: Emergency Info | Saint Francis High School
text:
is no immediate danger to our school but conditions off campus may pose a risk. This means it’s safer for students and staff to stay indoors.
Examples include:
- A police situation in the neighborhood
- Severe weather such as high winds or flooding
- Poor air quality due to smoke, hazardous materials or chemical spills in the area
What happens on campus:
- Normal classroom instruction continues as much as possible
- Students and educators remain inside and doors are secured
- No one enters or exits campus until the “all clear” is given
- Parents are notified when it is safe to do so, and given instructions about next steps
Lockdown
A lockdown is used when there is a potential or immediate threat to safety on or near campus. This might involve an intruder, police activity or other security concerns.
Examples include:
- An unauthorized person on campus
- An active threat or dangerous situation nearby
What happens on campus:
- All doors are locked and no one enters or exits campus until the “all clear” is given
- Students move to a secure area of the classroom, away from windows and doors
- The campus remains silent while law enforcement responds

- Students move to a secure area of the classroom, away from windows and doors

Evacuation
An evacuation is used when it is necessary to move students and educators off campus or away from a specific area due to a safety concern.
Examples include:
- Fire, smoke, gas leaks or utility failures on campus
- Structural damage to a building
- Any situation where remaining in place is unsafe
What happens on campus:
- Students and educators are directed to leave the buildings in a calm and orderly manner and relocate to a designated safe area on or off campus
- Attendance is taken to ensure all students are accounted for
- Emergency personnel assess the situation
- Parents are notified when it is safe to do so, and given instructions about reunification or next steps

title: English Placement Considerations | Class of 2030 | Saint Francis High School
text:
Freshmen students take English 1 or English 1 Honors.
A national score of 85% on HSPT reading is required for placement into honors. The main difference between the courses lies in pacing, independence, and depth of analysis. English 1H moves at a more accelerated pace with fewer practice opportunities before assessments, requires more independent reading (30-50 pages nightly vs. 20-30 pages in English 1), and expects students to develop original analytical arguments with minimal guidance. Both courses cover essential foundations in reading and writing, but 1H approaches literature more rigorously from the start.

Additional Placement Considerations
For both English 1 and English 1H students, the transition to high school English represents several shifts that can initially challenge freshmen. Some students experience frustration when moving from primarily in-class reading to managing independent reading schedules with objective comprehension quizzes. Additionally, the shift from effort-based to skills-based grading often surprises students who are accustomed to receiving grades primarily for completing work. In high school English, assignments are assessed on demonstrated mastery of specific skills rather than just completion. Writing expectations also increase substantially - while middle school may have emphasized personal reflection or creative expression, high school analytical writing requires evidence-based arguments and deeper textual analysis. Students sometimes struggle with this transition from sharing opinions to defending analytical claims with specific evidence.

cal writing requires evidence-based arguments and deeper textual analysis. Students sometimes struggle with this transition from sharing opinions to defending analytical claims with specific evidence.
To support this adjustment, both English 1 and 1H, provide practice opportunities that allow students to develop these skills before major assessments. One of the distinctions between 1 and 1H is the number of practice opportunities where 1H generally have fewer due to the accelerated nature of the course.
Students in English 1 and 1H are encouraged to view practice assignments as valuable learning opportunities and to seek teacher feedback during the learning process, such as during Collaboration, rather than waiting until after receiving grades on major assessments. Students who actively engage with practice assignments and request clarification early in the learning process typically have a smoother transition to high school English expectations.

English 1H is designed to challenge students who feel willing to take an academic risk in pursuit of a more rigorous approach to literature, and as such students are expected to adjust to reading and writing at an advanced level from the start of the course. text:
Background & Purpose
Educational research and our own experience have shown that traditional grading practices do not always provide an accurate picture of student learning. In particular, lessons learned during the pandemic highlighted the need for grading systems that better reflect students’ understanding and mastery of course learning objectives.
Saint Francis adapted equitable grading practices to focus grades on demonstrated learning rather than point accumulation. By incorporating both formative and summative assessments, students are given opportunities to practice, receive feedback and demonstrate mastery over time. Our most recent revision also seeks to strengthen our students’ executive functioning and planning skills necessary for college and career.
These practices encourage our students to take ownership of their learning, embrace challenges and develop resilience through reflection and revision. Aligned with our commitment to educating the whole person, equitable grading supports the development of confident, independent learners who are prepared to apply these skills well beyond the classroom.
Learning Objectives

text:
tment to educating the whole person, equitable grading supports the development of confident, independent learners who are prepared to apply these skills well beyond the classroom.
Learning Objectives
Skill-based learning objectives are stated in lesson plans and clearly communicated to students throughout the lesson. Students know how they will demonstrate mastery of the skills and how they will be assessed.
Formative vs. Summative Assessment
Students can interpret their progress toward these learning objectives in a mistake-friendly manner with formative assessment. Formative assessments help monitor student learning and allow teachers to offer feedback as students progress toward objectives. Examples:
- HOMEWORK for the purpose of practice, preparation and extension.
- QUIZZES serve to assess students’ knowledge and comprehension while building toward higher-order skill development.
- FEEDBACK in both narrative and quantitative form on formative assessments to prepare students to complete summative assessments of the same objectives.
When students wrap up a unit, they will demonstrate their mastery of the objectives through summative assessments.

text:

When students wrap up a unit, they will demonstrate their mastery of the objectives through summative assessments.
- Summative assessments vary by discipline and by skills asked to demonstrate. The summative assessment evaluates student learning to determine the extent to which students have met the learning objectives. Examples include projects that build over time, portfolios, podcasts, essays or research papers, performance tasks, end of unit projects or tests.
Revisable vs. Non-revisable
A goal of equitable grading is to allow students to continue to master learning objectives. Revisions or retakes allow students to revisit their learning and work towards mastery if they do not demonstrate proficiency on the first attempt.
Students who score below 75% may retake or revise eligible assessments. Before a second attempt, students will be expected to reflect on their progress toward the learning objectives and follow department and course-level guidelines. Retakes or revised work is eligible for up to 75% credit.

text:

We allow a portion of work to remain non-revisable, in order to reduce pressure on students to achieve perfection on every assignment and to ensure they have time to focus on new learning across their classes.
Due Dates & Flexible Submissions
The principles of equitable grading are rooted in flexibility, the idea being that the grade reflects the learning rather than the timing. At the same time, due dates do reflect a reality of the world of work and allow students to complete a cycle of learning before moving on to learning new material.
In order to strike a balance between flexibility and accountability, the flexible submission policy provides students the opportunity to request two additional calendar days to submit out-of-class work without penalty. Students can make two flexible submission requests per class in each semester. Work submitted after two calendar days will be docked 10% per day late, up to 50%.

Students are always expected to complete in-class assessments (exams, timed writing, etc.) during class time on the day assigned.
Additional Details
- EXTRA CREDIT: In keeping with the goal for students’ grades to reflect their mastery of the learning objectives, “extra credit” will not be used.
- GROUP GRADING: Collaboration is a meaningful skill and should continue to be developed; however, group work will not contribute to an individual’s grade. There is no “group grade."
- MINIMUM GRADES: Graded work turned in will earn at least a 50%. Missing work will be issued a 40%.
- INTEGRITY VIOLATIONS: Students found to be in violation of academic integrity with a cheating or plagiarism offense will be issued a referral to the Deans and will be subject to disciplinary action, which has implications for the student’s ability to do a revision/retake or complete the assignment, depending on the level of the offense.

Using a calendar to block out time for scheduled activities and necessary tasks can help avoid overscheduling to allow for unstructured time. Research shows that play time, down time, and family time (PDF) is critical for a teenager’s health--and for that of adults! Play time is time for students to engage in an activity that they genuinely like to do. It is important that this time is unstructured. It could be taking the dog for a walk, going on a hike, reading a new book, going outside to take pictures, or any other activity that a student chooses to do with their free time. Free time is a concept that many teenagers overlook, but playtime is important for teenagers to continue building neural connections and to increase self-awareness and self-exploration.

From Across the Bay Area to Saint Francis
Our students come from communities throughout the Bay Area, bringing together families from across the Peninsula, South Bay, East Bay and beyond. That reach is part of what makes the Saint Francis community so vibrant—and we know that getting to and from campus is an important part of every family’s day.
Whether your student travels by public transit, bike, carpool or a combination of options, there are a number of ways to make the daily trip to Saint Francis work for your family. Explore the resources below to find the transportation option that works best for you.

title: Grades & Progress Reports | Understanding Grades & Progerss Reports | Academics Dashboard | Parents  | Saint Francis High School
text:
Throughout the year, progress reports provide regular snapshots of how things are going, along with natural moments to celebrate what's working and plan for what's next. Grades can feel like a big deal, and we want them to feel clear rather than confusing. This page walks you through what each report includes, who can see it, how you'll receive it and how to support your student if a grade raises questions. As always, we're here to help.
How the Grading Year Works
Each semester includes three grading checkpoints: a six-week Academic Progress report, a 12-week progress report, and the Semester Report card at 18 weeks. Only semester grades appear on a student's transcript and count toward their cumulative GPA. The progress reports along the way are snapshots designed to help everyone stay informed and on track.
The Six-Week Academic Progress Report
The six-week Academic Progress report reflects student progress in each class as of September 25, and it is finalized by October 1.
What's included

title: Grades & Progress Reports | Understanding Grades & Progerss Reports | Academics Dashboard | Parents  | Saint Francis High School
text:
and on track.
The Six-Week Academic Progress Report
The six-week Academic Progress report reflects student progress in each class as of September 25, and it is finalized by October 1.
What's included
These grades include summative assessments and formative work, if applicable, from the first six weeks of school. Keep in mind that the feedback-revision cycle on the first summatives may not yet be complete at this point, so some grades may still change as revisions are submitted and graded.
Why it matters
Even though it doesn't appear on the transcript, this benchmark gives students and educators a chance to assess progress and to check academic eligibility for extracurricular activities. To be eligible, a student must maintain a 2.0 GPA or higher. It's also a great opportunity to connect with your student about the strategies that are working, the challenges they may be facing, and any support they might need moving forward.
Who can see it
School administrators, teachers, parents, students, and counselors all have access to the six-week progress report.
A Note for Families of Seniors

School administrators, teachers, parents, students, and counselors all have access to the six-week progress report.
A Note for Families of Seniors
In most cases, six-week progress report grades are not sent to colleges and universities. The official marking period for grades is the semester. Semester grades will be sent to colleges that require a mid-year report, which includes grades through the 7th semester, and this can apply to both Early and Regular Decision admissions. A select few colleges will ask for a mid-semester progress report if the student has applied Early Action or Early Decision. In that situation, the counselor will consult with the student before sending any grades.
Receiving Reports
Parents and students will continue to receive emailed PDF reports once teachers have verified grades with the Academic Office. As we shift away from mailed reports, we are also piloting Doc Viewer in Schoology as a place to view your student's Progress Reports and Semester Report cards.

Didn't get your report?
Progress reports are sent directly from the reporting system's email provider, not through our school's email system. To keep the email out of your spam folder, please add the domain brightarrow.com to your whitelist or safe sender list.
Supporting Your Student
If a grade concerns you, remember that a progress report is a snapshot in time and is subject to change. Before drawing conclusions, it helps to consider the total number of graded assignments, any revisions that haven't yet been submitted or graded, any missing assignments that may be affecting the grade, and whether your student is struggling in several areas or just one class. Schoology can help you take a deeper dive into the "why" behind a grade. Looking at these factors may ease your concerns, or it may reveal an opportunity to help your student take a proactive approach to their learning.

title: Grades & Transcripts | Online Courses | Summer at Saint Francis | Saint Francis High School
text:
Overall Grade & Actual Grade
Please watch the video below about the "student experience" with Imagine Learning (Edgenuity). At 45-sec it goes into detail about pacing and grading.
The actual grade is the grade the student has received for the semester with all missing assignments factored into that grade. So if a student did 5 out of 10 assignments for the year and scored a 100% on each of those 5 assignments the grade overall is going to show as 50% because of those 5 missing assignments.
The overall grade is the grade the student has received for the semester without any missing assignments factored into that score. So if a student did 5 out of 10 assignments for the year and scored a 100% on each of those 5 assignments the grade overall is going to show as 100%.
If you are behind pace, your actual grade will be lower than your overall grade. You will receive the "actual grade" on your transcript. The below scale is for transcripts.

text:
Gratitude in the Holy Cross Tradition
At the heart of the Holy Cross charism is a spirit of gratitude—an essential value and the lens through which we recognize the gifts of education, community, and faith.
As modeled by the Brothers of Holy Cross, we believe that expressing thanks is not just a gesture but a way of living. Just as we teach our students to appreciate their blessings, we strive to model gratitude in our relationships with them, our alumni, families and donors.
Whether you are part of a giving society or give as a part of our broader donor base, your generosity helps advance the future of Saint Francis and enriches the lives of our students. Thank you!
Giving Societies
President’s Circle
The President’s Circle honors the generous commitment of donors who give $5,000 or more within a school year in support of Saint Francis High School. As a member, you are among our trusted partners in providing extraordinary learning opportunities for our students each year, allowing them to reach their maximum potential.

title: Guidance & Counseling | Academics | Saint Francis High School
text:
The Saint Francis Guidance and College Counseling Center provides a comprehensive program designed to assist students through their personal and academic journeys, while helping them identifying their aspirations for the future, including college and career.
College Counseling Social & Emotional Learning
Our unique model directs freshman counselors to focus on supporting our newest Lancers in the adjustment to high school, provide academic and personal counseling and ensure a smooth transition in this important year.
Freshman counselors use small groups to explore topics including making connections, time management and an introduction to counseling. Freshman counselors remain available to freshmen for individual counseling appointments, and they will also meet individually with students to discuss academic planning for the Sophomore year.

Students in their sophomore year will then transition to their assigned Guidance and College Counselor, who they will work with through the senior year. Through a variety of classroom presentations, group meetings, and individual guidance, students are assisted in selecting colleges that match their academic goals and interests. The upper level counselors advocate for students and provide support for their academic and social-emotional needs; they are also a student’s guide to their college search and application process.

title: Guidance & College Counseling Dashboard | Student Dashboard | Students | Saint Francis High School
text:
The Saint Francis Guidance & College Counseling team offers far more than support in choosing a college. Our program is an educational partnership designed to help students discover their interests, clarify their goals and thoughtfully plan for life beyond Saint Francis.
We work closely with each student to understand their academic strengths, personal preferences and aspirations for the future. Through classroom presentations, small group sessions and individualized guidance, students are supported in exploring options and identifying colleges that align with their goals and values.
Follow us on Instagram for the latest updates and helpful reminders @sfhscounseling!

title: Health and Fitness Clothing | Class of 2030 | Saint Francis High School
text:
Health & Fitness Program & Clothing Information
All freshman students will participate in either a semester or full year of Health and Fitness during the 2026–27 school year. To ensure every student is prepared from the first day, Saint Francis will provide each student with required health and fitness clothing and a lock.
Families will submit sizing information through the PowerSchool database form, which allows us to place orders on your behalf. Clothing and locks will then be distributed by Health and Fitness teachers on the first full day of classes in August.
Sizing & Fit
All Health and Fitness clothing is unisex. A detailed size chart is available to help guide your selection, and we recommend reviewing it carefully when submitting your form. Please note that shirts tend to run slightly large.
Making Updates or Asking Questions
If you need help selecting sizes or have specific questions, you’re welcome to reach out directly to Lisa Pazmany at lisapazmany@sfhs.com for guidance.
If you’ve already submitted your form and need to make any changes, the Admissions Office can assist you. Please contact lisapazmany@sfhs.com, and they will help update your information.

title: History | About Saint Francis | Saint Francis High School
text:
Early History
In 1954, the Brothers of Holy Cross envisioned a Catholic college preparatory high school in Mountain View. A year later, Saint Francis High School opened with 45 students, introducing the Holy Cross philosophy of educating the whole person.
From its earliest days, Saint Francis emphasized academics, faith, and extracurriculars—launching a band, theater program, student newspaper, and athletics. Rooted in tradition and driven by innovation, Saint Francis continues to develop leaders of character, prepared to serve and succeed in an ever-changing world.
| Merger with Holy Cross High School Holy Cross, an all-girls high school founded and staffed by Sisters of the Holy Cross, opened in 1957 on Miramonte Avenue, within a mile of Saint Francis High School. In an effort to expand educational programming and facilities and extend the Holy Cross educational mission, the schools joined forces to create a co-educational learning environment serving nearly 1,200 young men and women in 1972. The consolidation of these schools was a catalyst for rapid and significant change on campus, marking the beginning of a new era for Saint Francis. |  |

The Holy Cross Achievers (HCA) Program
